candidates.statement: This guidance provides recommendations for clinical trials designed to assess the adhesion 17 performance of transdermal and topical delivery systems (collectively referred to as TDS). 18 Adhesion performance is defined in this guidance as whether the TDS fully adheres to the 19 subject in the applied location for the duration of use of the TDS. Adhesion performance can 20 affect both safety and effectiveness of TDS products because adhesion failures can result in 21 reduced effectiveness caused by suboptimal dosing or potentially increased exposure when a new 22 TDS needs to be applied sooner than the scheduled dose. Additionally, partial or full detachment 23 of a TDS from a patient’s skin may result in unintentional exposure of the active pharmaceutical 24 ingredient to a partner, child, or other individual, potentially exposing them to the drug’s 25 toxicity. Adhesion performance may also inform the Dosage and Administration section of 26 labeling. 27
candidates.context: The recommendations in this guidance relate to studies to be submitted in support of a new drug 29 application (NDA) or supplemental new drug application (sNDA) for human prescription and 30 nonprescription drug products under Section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act 31 (21 U.S.C. § 355) and 21 CFR Part 314. Because biological products are often more complex 32 and of a higher molecular weight, it is likely that these products would not be absorbed across 33 the skin, requiring a different approach for administration, so they are outside the scope of this 34 guidance. 35

candidates.statement: Transdermal delivery systems are designed to deliver an active pharmaceutical ingredient across 51 the skin and into systemic circulation, whereas topical delivery systems are designed to deliver 52 the active ingredient to local tissue. 2 The amount of drug delivered into and through the patient’s 53 skin from a TDS depends, in part, on the surface area in direct contact with the TDS. The TDS 54 should remain consistently and uniformly adherent to the patient’s skin throughout the duration 55 of wear. During the product’s wear period, a TDS is reasonably expected to encounter torsional 56 strains arising from body movements, changes in environmental temperature or humidity such as 57 daily exposure to water (e.g., during routine showering), and contact with clothing, bedding, or 58 other surfaces. When a TDS loses its adhesion during wear, the amount of drug delivered to the 59 patient may be reduced, potentially compromising effectiveness. 60
candidates.context: TDS development has evolved over the years, especially with respect to expected adhesion 62 performance. TDS products developed today may use technologies that were not available when 63 the first TDS products were approved. This guidance takes these developments into 64 consideration. When final, this draft guidance will expand upon the recommendation for in vivo 65 adhesion studies in section V., Special Topics, subsection A., Product Adhesion Considerations, 66 in the draft guidance for industry Transdermal and Topical Delivery Systems – Product 67 Development and Quality Considerations (November 2019). 3 68

candidates.statement: Although the inpatient setting of a clinical wear trial informs the adhering capability of the TDS, 233 the actual user experience may differ. Therefore, in addition to the clinical wear trial described 234 above, if subsequent larger clinical trials are conducted (e.g., a phase 2 or phase 3 trial), sponsors 235 should collect information on product adhesion. Sponsors should obtain this information by 236 using patient diaries describing their user experience with product adhesion. This information is 237 especially important when a novel transdermal or topical system is being studied, when the TDS 238 contains a drug substance (e.g., an opioid) that has a higher risk associated with accidental 239 exposure, or when the clinical wear trial may not adequately capture use in the intended 240 population.
